The National Patient Register (Landspatientregisteret, LPR) is where hospital
diagnoses, contacts and procedures come from. It holds inpatient contacts from
1977, and outpatient, emergency department and psychiatric contacts from 1995.
Private hospitals and clinics report through a separate system, see [Private
hospitals](extract-from-lpr.qmd#private-hospitals).

Read this page before you write code against LPR. It explains how the register
is laid out: the two periods (LPR2 and LPR3), which tables hold what, how the
diagnosis codes and diagnosis types work, and the breaks in 1994, 1995 and 2019
that change what a count means. When you are done you know which tables your
study period needs and which filters to apply. The code is on the next page,
[Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
**In short:** LPR changed format in 2019: use LPR2 (up to March 2019) and LPR3
(after) and combine them. All ICD codes carry a `D` prefix you usually strip,
and you choose diagnosis types (A/B for outcomes; G for baseline comorbidity
exists only in 1995-2003). LPR2 contacts that never closed are only in separate
open-contact tables ([why](#lpr2-open-contacts)).
:::


## LPR is split into two periods

In early 2019 LPR changed format, from LPR2 to LPR3. Two dates matter, and they
are not the same thing:

- **When the hospitals switched their reporting.** Region Hovedstaden, Region
  Sjælland and Region Midtjylland switched to LPR3 on the weekend of 2-3
  February 2019, Region Nordjylland and Region Syddanmark on the weekend of 2-3
  March 2019 ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's data quality report on LPR3, April
  2019](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/media/16452/Datakvalitetsrapport%20om%20LPR3%20pr.%2012.%20april%202019.pdf)).
- **Where DST's LPR2 files end.** `lpr_adm`, `lpr_diag` and the other LPR2
  registers at DST end on 31 March 2019 ([DST's register
  overview](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html)).

A study period that crosses early 2019 needs both systems, combined.

  |                        | LPR2 somatic                    | LPR2 psychiatric         | LPR3                                 |
  | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
  | **Period**             | 1977 to 31 March 2019           | 1995 to 31 March 2019    | February or March 2019 and onwards   |
  | **Kinds of contact**   | inpatient only before 1995⁴     | all, from 1995           | all                                  |
  | **Contact register**   | `lpr_adm`                       | `t_psyk_adm`             | `lpr_a_kontakt`                      |
  | **Diagnosis register** | `lpr_diag`                      | `t_psyk_diag`            | `lpr_a_diagnose`                     |
  | **Covers psychiatry**  | No                              | Yes                      | Yes (both combined)                  |
  | **Join key**           | `recnum`                        | `recnum`¹                | `dw_ek_kontakt`                      |
  | **Date column**        | `d_inddto` (Date)               | `d_inddto` (Date)        | `kont_starttidspunkt` (datetime)²    |
  | **pnr column**         | `pnr`                           | `pnr`³                   | `pnr`                                |
  | **Diagnosis code**     | `c_diag`                        | `c_diag`                 | `diag_kode`                          |
  | **Diagnosis type**     | `c_diagtype`                    | `c_diagtype`             | `diag_kode_type`                     |
  | **Contact type**       | `c_pattype` (`"0"` = inpatient) | `c_pattype`              | `kont_type` (`"ALCA00"` = physical attendance) |

¹ ³ These are DST's names. Check whether your variables have been changed during
delivery or data preprocessing: in DARTER the join key arrives as `k_recnum` in
`t_psyk_adm` and `v_recnum` in `t_psyk_diag`, and the person column as `v_cpr`.
Check `colnames()` and rename to `recnum` and `pnr` before joining. ² datetime
format - convert with `as.Date()`.

⁴ **LPR2 does not hold the same kinds of contact in all years.** From 1977
through 1994 it holds inpatient contacts only. Outpatient and emergency
department contacts, and contacts at psychiatric departments, are in it from
1995. Some outpatient contacts were reported already in 1994, but not
completely ([Schmidt et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S91125);
[Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR
documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5)).
A study that counts outpatient or emergency contacts therefore cannot start
before 1995.

This table lists what the registers contain, not what your project was given.
Run `colnames()` on your own extract before you build anything on a column here -
`c_pattype` in particular is often left out (see [Patient type](#patienttype)).

### Contact table and diagnosis table: every extract is a join {#contact-and-diagnosis-tables}

LPR splits each hospital contact into two tables. The **contact register**
(e.g. `lpr_adm`) has one row per contact with `pnr`, dates and hospital, but not
the diagnoses. The **diagnosis register** (e.g. `lpr_diag`) has one row per
diagnosis with the ICD code, but neither `pnr` nor a date. One contact can have
several diagnoses. You join the two on the contact key (`recnum` in LPR2,
`dw_ek_kontakt` in LPR3) to get `pnr`, date and diagnosis in one table. The
recipes in [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd) are built on that join.

Operations and procedures work the same way: `lpr_sksopr` (LPR2) has the SKS
code (SKS is the Danish health care classification system) and `recnum`, but not
`pnr` or date, so it is joined to `lpr_adm` when you want to find who had an
operation and when.

### Psychiatry: separate tables in LPR2, combined in LPR3 {#psychiatry}

Before 2019, contacts at psychiatric departments and their diagnoses (typically
F-codes such as dementia and depression) were stored in separate registers
(`t_psyk_adm`, `t_psyk_diag`). The structure resembles somatic LPR2, but column names can
differ (see the table footnotes above). LPR3 combines both: somatic and
psychiatric contacts and diagnoses are in the same tables, and no separate
psychiatric query is needed.

Psychiatric data older than 1995 exists but is not part of a standard LPR
extract, see [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd#psyk-before-1995).

### Timeline of the LPR tables

```{mermaid}
gantt
    title LPR registers
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM
    axisFormat  %Y
    section LPR2 somatic
    lpr_adm + lpr_diag (inpatient only)              :done,   1977-01, 1995-01
    lpr_adm + lpr_diag (plus outpatient + emergency) :done,   1995-01, 2019-03
    section LPR2 psychiatric
    t_psyk_adm + t_psyk_diag                         :done,   1995-01, 2019-03
    section LPR_A files
    rows tagged LPR1 / LPR2 / MiniPAS (overlap)      :crit,   2017-01, 2019-03
    rows tagged LPR3                                 :active, 2019-03, 2027-01
```

The figure shows two breaks that are easy to miss: outpatient, emergency and
psychiatric contacts only start in 1995 (footnote 4 above), and the LPR_A files
overlap the LPR2 files from 2017 to early 2019 (the callout below).

### LPR3 is delivered in the LPR_A files

You access LPR3 through the LPR_A files (`lpr_a_kontakt`, `lpr_a_diagnose`).

::: {.callout-important #lpr-a-format}
**Use the LPR_A files, and filter them. Two things, both easy to get wrong.**

1. **LPR_A, not LPR_F.** LPR3 has been delivered as two sets of tables: the
   older LPR_F (`kontakter`, `diagnoser`, `forloeb`) and the current LPR_A
   (`lpr_a_kontakt`, `lpr_a_diagnose`). DST released LPR_A in June 2025 and has
   closed LPR_F for ordering. DST writes that the LPR_A tables largely
   correspond to the LPR_F tables but hold considerably more variables (LPR_A
   has 12 tables, LPR_F had 14), and that LPR_A, unlike LPR_F, also holds LPR2
   rows from 2017-2019 ([DST, Nyt om grunddata, 2nd quarter
   2025](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/nyt-og-meddelelser/2025/nyt-om-grunddata-2-kvartal-2025)).
   Every example on this site uses `lpr_a_*`. An older project may have both
   sets in its folder. They hold the same LPR3 contacts, so use one of them:
   stacking both gives you duplicated rows.
2. **LPR_A holds four reporting systems in one table.** Besides LPR3 contacts,
   `lpr_a_kontakt` and `lpr_a_diagnose` hold contacts from the older systems
   that ended in 2017 or later. Every row is tagged by
   `lprindberetningssystem` (reporting system): `LPR1`, `LPR2`, `MiniPAS`
   (records from private hospitals) and `LPR3`. DST says so in its [remark on
   LPR_A_KONTAKT](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/Bemaerkning/LPR_A_KONTAKT%20-%20Landspatientregistret%20%28LPR3%29%20-Kontaktoplysninger%20omkring%20de%20enkelte%20kontakter.html).
   That is why the files reach back to 2017, before LPR3 reporting began in
   early 2019: "LPR3" as a period and "LPR_A" as a file are two different
   things. Filter both `lpr_a_kontakt` and `lpr_a_diagnose` with
   `lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3"`, or a contact already counted from
   `lpr_adm` gets counted again from its `LPR2`-tagged copy in here. The
   join key does not carry the reporting system, so filtering the contact
   table alone leaves the diagnosis rows unchecked.

   The filter can also drop real contacts: if your project's `lpr_adm` ends
   before DST's own LPR2 files do (31 March 2019), the `LPR2`-tagged rows are
   the only copy of the contacts in between. And private-hospital contacts
   (MiniPAS) need a register of their own. Both are explained, with a check
   to run on your own delivery, in [Extract from
   LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd#lpr3-filter-caveat). Read that before you trust
   a count that spans 2019.

*(The LPR_F data model is documented in [Vejledning til
LPR3_F](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/media/16364/Vejledning%20til%20LPR3_F.pdf)
if you have inherited a project that used it. LPR_A documentation is still
incomplete.)*
:::

## Open contacts are in separate LPR2 tables {#lpr2-open-contacts}

`lpr_adm` and `lpr_diag` hold **closed** contacts, filed by the year the contact
ended: the 2016 file holds the contacts that ended in 2016, including ones that
started years earlier. A contact that has not ended is kept in a separate set of
tables with the same structure, the *uafsluttede* (open) contacts. DST delivers
them as `UAF_ADM`, `UAF_DIAG`, `UAF_SKSOPR`, `UAF_SKSUBE` and a `UAF_` table for
most of the other LPR2 tables ([DST's register
overview](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html)).

The open tables are filed by the year the contact **started**, and the contact
stays in them for every year it is open. Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's example: a
contact that starts in 2014 and ends in 2016 is in the open tables for 2014 and
2015, and in the regular tables for 2016 ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR
documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5),
section "Datastruktur").

The register holds open outpatient courses started from 1995 and open
admissions from 2015 (same source, "Periode"). Some outpatient contacts run for
a long time, for example a course where the patient comes back for regular
check-ups, and some are only closed when the patient dies. An open contact has
no discharge date, so `d_uddto` is empty ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's extraction
guide](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/Media/638675370025223404/Udtrek-Landspatientregisteret.pdf)).

**What happened to open contacts when LPR2 stopped.** At the switch to LPR3 in
February and March 2019, the public hospitals had to close each open LPR2
contact, either for good or by closing it in LPR2 and opening it again in LPR3.
A contact closed this way ended in 2019, so it is in `lpr_adm`. Not every
contact was closed: Sundhedsdatastyrelsen counted just under 192,000 LPR2
contacts still open on 26 September 2020 ([data quality report on the
transition, 2 October
2020](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/media/16445/Datakvalitetsrapport%20om%20LPR%202019%20_%20overgangen%20fra%20LPR2%20til%20LPR3.pdf),
section 6.1.2). DST's `UAF_ADM2019` has about 167,000 rows ([DST's dataset
list](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/Datasaetlister/UAF_ADM%20-%20Landspatientregistret%20uafsluttede%20kontakter%20-%20administrative%20oplysninger.html)).

::: {.callout-important}
**A contact that never closed is not in `lpr_adm` or `lpr_diag` at all.** It is
only in the open tables. If you read only `lpr_adm` and `lpr_diag`, you miss its
diagnoses. A first-diagnosis date can then come out too late, and a person who
already had the disease can stay in the cohort when you exclude prevalent
cases. Sundhedsdatastyrelsen gives three reasons contacts stayed open: some
are so old that the hospitals' current IT systems cannot reach them, some were
closed but then reported again by mistake without an end date, and for some
the closing report failed (data quality report, section 6.1.2).
:::

**Stacking the tables counts a contact more than once.** A contact open for
three years is in three yearly open tables, and once it ends it is also in
`lpr_adm`. `recnum` does not tell you which rows are the same contact:
Sundhedsdatastyrelsen states that it is unique only within one update of the
register and can change or be reused. Its key for a contact is hospital,
department, patient type, person, and the date, hour and minute the contact
started (`c_sgh`, `c_afd`, `c_pattype`, `pnr`, `d_inddto`, `v_indtime`,
`v_indminut`). That is also the key it tells you to use to find the same
contacts again in a later extract (LPR documentation, "Enhed"; extraction
guide, "Et levende register").

The simplest way round this is to read only the **last year** of the open
tables. Under the filing rule above, those are the contacts that were still
open when DST's copy was made, and none of them is in an `lpr_adm` taken from
the same copy. That is what the recipes in [Extract from
LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd#one-outcome) do. Before 2014, an open outpatient
course could also carry provisional diagnoses (type `M`, see [Diagnosis
types](#diagtype)), which an A and B filter leaves out.

**Psychiatric LPR2 does not have this split.** Sundhedsdatastyrelsen keeps
psychiatric contacts in tables that are not divided by year and hold both
closed and open contacts ([LPR
documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5),
"Datastruktur"), and DST delivers `PSYK_ADM` as one dataset ([DST's dataset
list](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/Datasaetlister/PSYK_ADM%20-%20Landspatientregistret%20psykiatri%20-%20administrative%20oplysninger.html)).
Open psychiatric contacts are therefore already in `t_psyk_adm`, with an empty
`d_uddto`.

## ICD codes and the D-prefix

ICD-10 (International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision) is the WHO's
system for classifying diseases and conditions. Hospital diagnoses in Denmark
have been coded with ICD-10 since 1994 ([earlier years are ICD-8](#icd8)), e.g.
`G30` for Alzheimer's disease and `F00` for dementia in Alzheimer's.

ICD-10 codes in LPR have a prepended `"D"`: `"DG30"` (Alzheimer's), `"DF00"`
(dementia), `"DI21"` (acute myocardial infarction). The D is a Danish addition
from SKS, not part of the WHO code.

The examples on this site strip the D-prefix before comparing codes, so that a
code list reads like the ICD-10 codes in a paper and can be reused across
registers:

```r
mutate(icd3 = substr(c_diag, 2, 4)) # "DG30" → "G30" (3-digit code)
mutate(icd4 = substr(c_diag, 2, 5)) # "DI219" → "I219" (4-digit code)
```

`substr(x, start, stop)` keeps characters from position `start` up to and
including `stop` (counted from 1). `substr(c_diag, 2, 4)` skips position 1 (the
D-prefix) and keeps characters 2, 3 and 4: `"DG30"` → `"G30"`. Use 2 to 5 for
4-digit codes: `"DI219"` → `"I219"`.

### Only the patient registers have the D-prefix {#d-prefix-not-everywhere}

The prefix belongs to the patient registers. Other registers store the plain
WHO code, and stripping the first character there removes a real one:

  | Register | Column | What it holds | Example |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | LPR2, LPR3, psychiatric LPR | `c_diag`, `diag_kode`, `adiag` | D-prefixed | `DE119` |
  | Cause of death (`dodsaars`, `dodsaasg`) | `c_dod1`, `c_dod_1a` | plain | `E119` |
  | Cancer register | `c_icd10` | plain | `C509` |

Run `substr(x, 2, 4)` on `"E119"` and you get `"119"`. It matches nothing, it
raises no error, and the result looks like an empty subgroup rather than a bug.

**A leading D is not always a prefix.** ICD-10 has codes of its own that begin
with D: `D46` (myelodysplastic syndromes) and `D32` (benign meningeal tumour)
are whole codes. In the cancer register they are stored exactly like that.
Strip the "prefix" and `D46` becomes `46`.

### Before 1994 the codes are ICD-8 {#icd8}

LPR2 starts in 1977, and Denmark did not move to ICD-10 until 1994
([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR
documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5)).
The early years hold ICD-8: pure digits, no letter and no decimal point, so
446.30 is stored as `44630`.

You get no error or warning from this. An ICD-10 code list matches no rows
before 1994, and `substr(c_diag, 2, 4)` on `"44630"` returns `"463"`, which is
not a code in any classification. A study whose period starts before 1994 reads
two classifications out of one column and needs a code list for each.

The same applies to `dodsaars`, which runs from 1970 and changes over in the
same year.

## Diagnosis types {#diagtype}

LPR2 (`c_diagtype`) has six diagnosis types, and three of them were only in use
for some years:

  | Code | Meaning                                                                          | In use in LPR2 | When to include               |
  | ---- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ----------------------------- |
  | A    | Action diagnosis (primary diagnosis) - the main reason for the contact           | 1977 onwards   | Yes, for outcomes             |
  | B    | Secondary diagnosis - additional condition present                               | 1977 onwards   | Yes, for outcomes             |
  | G    | Underlying condition (grundmorbus), when different from the action diagnosis     | 1995-2003      | Only for baseline comorbidity |
  | H    | Referral diagnosis - given by the referring unit as the reason for referral      | 1995 onwards   | Usually not (see below)       |
  | M    | Provisional diagnosis - only for ongoing somatic outpatient contacts             | 1998-2013      | Usually not (see below)       |
  | C    | Complication                                                                     | 2002-2013      | Decide for your study         |

The codes and years are from Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's [code sheet for
LPR](https://www.esundhed.dk/-/media/Files/Dokumentation/Landspatientregisteret/5_Kodeark_LPR---pdf.ashx);
the explanations of A, H and M follow [Schmidt et al.
2015](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S91125). G was voluntary to record in
1995-2001, was recorded only for psychiatric patients in 2002-2003, and is not
used after 2003 ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR
documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5)).

H and M are usually left out of outcome and comorbidity definitions: a referral
diagnosis is what the referring unit suspected, and a provisional diagnosis is
not final. That follows from what the two types are; it is not a rule from
Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, so say in your methods what you chose.

LPR3 (`diag_kode_type`) has only two diagnosis types: action diagnosis (A) and
secondary diagnosis (B) ([reporting guideline for LPR 2025, section
6.1.3](https://cdn.sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/Media/638955095432142451/LPR-indberetningsvejledning_2025_v.5.1.pdf)).

```r
# For outcomes and exclusion diagnoses:
filter(c_diagtype %in% c("A", "B"))

# For baseline comorbidity:
filter(c_diagtype %in% c("A", "B", "G")) # note: "G" only exists 1995-2003
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**Keep the type column in your extract.** Carry `c_diagtype` (in LPR3:
`diag_kode_type`) into your output, not just the diagnosis code. It costs one
column and lets you vary the case definition later (main analysis on A + B,
sensitivity analysis on A only or including G) without querying LPR again.
:::

## Patient type: inpatient, outpatient or emergency {#patienttype}

Some studies need to tell inpatient contacts apart from outpatient and
emergency-room visits, for example to count only admissions as an outcome.
LPR2 has a field for it, LPR3 does not, so you derive patient type differently
in the two.

::: {.callout-important}
**`c_pattype` and `c_indm` have to be in your extract.** DST documents both for
every year of LPR_ADM, but a delivery only contains the variables the project
ordered. In the DARTER delivery, for instance, `lpr_adm` has neither, while
`t_psyk_adm` has both - the same register family, two different extract scopes.

Run `colnames()` on your own `lpr_adm` first. If the columns are missing, no
filtering trick recovers them: you have to ask DST to add them to the delivery.
:::

Check the column names and codes below against your own extract with
`arrow::schema()` or `colnames()`, and look them up in [Overview of
registers](register-reference.qmd): the column names in LPR_A may differ from
the example. The pattern is adapted from [the Plana-Ripoll group's code on
OSF](https://osf.io/zhfyp/overview).

### Patient type in LPR2: `c_pattype`

Patient type is in `c_pattype`, but the coding changed twice
([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR
documentation](https://www.esundhed.dk/Dokumentation/DocumentationExtended?id=5),
under "Kendte databrud/ændringer", known data breaks):

- **Emergency room, 2014:** code `"3"` was discontinued, and emergency-room
  visits are from then on registered as `"2"` (outpatient) with an acute
  admission mode (`c_indm == "1"`).
- **Part-day patients, 2002:** code `"1"` was discontinued. After that,
  hospitals registered these patients differently: some as outpatients, some as
  inpatients. The code below groups `"1"` with inpatients; whichever you choose,
  inpatient counts are not directly comparable before and after 2002.

```r
library(dplyr) # mutate, case_when

lpr2_type <- lpr_adm %>% # your lpr_adm extract
  mutate(
    patienttype = case_when(
      c_pattype %in% c("0", "1") ~ "inpatient", # "0" full/admitted, "1" part-day
      c_pattype == "3" ~ "emergency", # explicit ER, discontinued in 2014
      c_pattype == "2" & c_indm == "1" ~ "emergency", # from 2014: "3" became "2" + acute
      c_pattype == "2" ~ "outpatient",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
```

### Patient type in LPR3: derived from duration

LPR3 has no `c_pattype`. The `kont_type` code `ALCA00` means physical
attendance (not admission): the patient came in, whether for an outpatient
visit or an admission. The other
contact types are `ALCA01` home or outreach visit, `ALCA03` virtual contact,
`ALCA10` death and `ALCA20` a pseudo-contact for reporting diagnoses only
(Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, [LPR reporting guide, Bilag
1](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638955095266548367/Bilag1_model_og_regler_v.5.1.pdf)).
The `prioritet` (priority) code `ATA1` means acute. The example below derives
patient type from the contact's duration plus an emergency-room marker
(`skadestue` is Danish for emergency room):

```r
library(dplyr) # filter, mutate, case_when

lpr3_type <- lpr3_k %>% # your lpr_a_kontakt extract, already fetched into R with collect() - datetime arithmetic is not reliable on a lazy table
  filter(kont_type == "ALCA00") %>% # physical attendances only; drops home visits, virtual, death and diagnosis-only contacts
  mutate(
    duration_hours = as.numeric(
      difftime(kont_sluttidspunkt, kont_starttidspunkt, units = "hours") # verify the end-time column name
    ),
    patienttype = case_when(
      duration_hours >= 8 ~ "inpatient", # >= 8 hours ~ admission
      enhedstype_ans == "skadestue" & prioritet == "ATA1" ~ "emergency", # acute ER
      TRUE ~ "outpatient"
    )
  )
```

**The 8-hour cut-off is a heuristic, not an official definition.** LPR3 has no
"inpatient" field. Other cut-offs are in use: DST's hospital statistics report
stays under and over 12 hours ([DST, documentation of the hospital utilisation
statistics](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/statistikdokumentation/sygehusbenyttelse/statistisk-behandling)).
Pick a threshold, write it in your methods, and clarify it with your data
manager.

## Retracted diagnoses in LPR3 (`senere_afkraeftet`)

LPR3 flags diagnoses that were later retracted in the column
`senere_afkraeftet` ("later disproved"). The filter used on this site:

```r
filter(is.na(senere_afkraeftet) | senere_afkraeftet != "Ja")
```

The `is.na()` part is needed. In R, `NA != "Ja"` returns `NA`, not `TRUE`, and
`filter()` drops rows where the condition is `NA`. `filter(senere_afkraeftet !=
"Ja")` alone would therefore remove every diagnosis with an empty flag. With
`is.na(...)` in front, the row is kept if the flag is empty or is not `"Ja"`.
The filter thus assumes that a diagnosis with an empty flag was not retracted.

## Diagnosis counts jump around 2019-2020 {#lpr3-spike}

The move to LPR3's contact-based model also changed how outpatient diagnoses
are registered, and this can distort diagnosis counts across the transition.

In LPR2, a course of outpatient visits was typically summarised with a
single (action) diagnosis for the whole course. In LPR3, each contact
can carry its own diagnoses. So a patient with 10 outpatient visits for
depression that produced one diagnosis row in LPR2 can produce ten rows
in LPR3: the same illness, many more registrations.

::: {.callout-important}
**Count-based analyses are clearly affected.** Number of contacts or
diagnoses per person per year, healthcare utilisation or recurrence measures,
episode counts, or anything comparing volume before and after 2019: the same
clinical course can turn into many more registrations, and the apparent
"spike" is a registration artifact, not a real change in disease incidence.

**For first- or last-diagnosis dates, part of the answer is documented.** In
principle, fragmentation alone should not change a "first diagnosis of X" date -
the earliest matching row is still the earliest row, whether the underlying
course produced one registration or ten. For courses that ran across the
transition, Sundhedsdatastyrelsen documents the following. About 27% of the 8.2
million forløbselementer (course elements) that the public hospitals reported
to LPR3 for 2019 are marked as transferred from LPR2. A transferred course
element starts at the time of the transition, and the LPR2 contact it continues
was closed at that time ([data quality report on the
transition](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/media/16445/Datakvalitetsrapport%20om%20LPR%202019%20_%20overgangen%20fra%20LPR2%20til%20LPR3.pdf),
section 6.1.2). So in LPR3 the course starts in 2019, and its earlier history
is on the LPR2 contact, which ended in 2019 with discharge mode `c_udm` = `M`
("afsluttet til LPR3", closed to LPR3) and is in `lpr_adm`. A
first-diagnosis date taken across LPR2 and LPR3 comes from that LPR2 contact,
as long as it is in your extract. Contacts that were never closed are a
separate case, see [Open contacts](#lpr2-open-contacts).

Sundhedsdatastyrelsen could link only about 58% of the transferred course
elements back to an LPR2 contact (81% if the hour is left out of the match),
and some course elements were marked as transferred without being so (same
report). **Test this on your own data before relying on it**: check whether a
first- or last-diagnosis date you compute shows any jump or shift around
2019-2020, the same way you check counts below.
:::

The visible effect, for a count-based analysis, is a spike in the number of
diagnoses around 2019-2020, present for most diagnoses, and visible even if
you restrict to the primary (action) diagnosis. It overlaps with COVID-19 in
2020, which makes the period even harder to interpret.

### Check your own diagnoses across the transition

There is no single agreed fix, and the problem is largest for analyses that
rely only on hospital diagnoses. Count the diagnoses used in your study per
calendar year and look at the result:

```r
library(dplyr)     # mutate, count, arrange
library(lubridate) # year
all_dx %>%
  # not `year`: that name belongs to the parquet partition column, and
  # assigning to it would overwrite it
  mutate(contact_year = lubridate::year(date_contact)) %>% # date_contact from your extract
  count(contact_year) %>%
  arrange(contact_year)
# plot n against contact_year and look for a jump around 2019-2020
```

Most diagnoses show the spike. A few are stable across the transition (type 1
diabetes, for example) and make a useful sanity check: if even a stable
diagnosis jumps in your data, something else is wrong.

For inspiration and for evaluating diagnostic stability across the transition,
see
[Aarhus-Psychiatry-Research/diagnostic-stability-lpr2-lpr3](https://github.com/Aarhus-Psychiatry-Research/diagnostic-stability-lpr2-lpr3)
(methodological inspiration, not code for reuse).
